claim: Shallow gradients of netrin-1 elicited highly polarized Pak1-mediated phosphorylation of shootin1 within growth cones.
source: Shallow gradients of netrin-1 elicited highly polarized Pak1-mediated phosphorylation of shootin1 within growth cones.
evidence: A 0.4% difference in netrin-1 concentration induced a 71% difference in shootin1a phosphorylation within growth cones (Figure 2C, D).

claim: Shootin1a directly interacts with L1-CAM.
source: As shown in Figure 3A, shootin1a directly interacted with L1-CAM-ICD.
evidence: In vitro binding assay using purified shootin1a and GST-tagged L1-CAM-ICD demonstrated direct interaction (Figure 3A).

claim: Shootin1a residues 1-125 are essential and sufficient to bind to L1-CAM.
source: An in vitro binding assay with purified proteins showed that residues 1–125 of shootin1a (shootin1a (1-125)) were essential and sufficient to bind to L1-CAM (Figure 5A).
evidence: In vitro binding assays with deletion mutants showed only shootin1a (1-125) bound to L1-CAM-ICD (Figure 5A).

claim: Shootin1a–L1-CAM interaction mediates netrin-1–induced F-actin–adhesion coupling.
source: These results suggest that shootin1a–L1-CAM interaction mediates netrin-1–induced F-actin–adhesion coupling.
evidence: Overexpression of shootin1a (1-125) increased F-actin flow velocity and abolished netrin-1-induced flow reduction (Figure 6A, B), indicating disruption of F-actin-adhesion coupling.

claim: Inhibition of shootin1a–L1-CAM interaction decreases traction forces and abolishes netrin-1–induced increase in traction forces.
source: Importantly, inhibition of the shootin1a–L1-CAM interaction by overexpressing myc-shootin1a (1-125) significantly decreased traction forces and abolished the netrin-1–induced increase in traction forces (Figure 6D).
evidence: Traction force microscopy showed that shootin1a (1-125) overexpression reduced forces and prevented netrin-1-induced force increase (Figure 6C, D).

claim: Netrin-1–induced axon attraction requires shootin1a.
source: Together, these data indicate that netrin-1–induced axon guidance of hippocampal neurons on an L1-CAM substrate requires shootin1a.
evidence: RNAi knockdown of shootin1a reduced axon outgrowth velocity from 26.1 to 5.6 μm/h and inhibited growth cone turning from 32.7° to 2.1° (Figure 7A-D). Similar results obtained with Shootin1 knockout neurons (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).

claim: Shootin1a–L1-CAM interaction is required for netrin-1–induced axon guidance.
source: These data suggest that the interaction between shootin1a and L1-CAM mediates netrin-1–induced axon guidance.
evidence: Overexpression of EGFP-shootin1a (1-125) reduced axon outgrowth velocity and inhibited growth cone turning toward netrin-1 source (Figure 7E, F, Figure 7—figure supplement 3).

claim: Polarized phosphorylation of shootin1a within growth cones is required for axon turning induced by netrin-1 gradients.
source: Furthermore, disturbance of the spatially regulated shootin1a phosphorylation within growth cones inhibited axon turning, but not axon outgrowth, induced by netrin-1 gradients.
evidence: Expression of RNAi-refractory shootin1a-DD (constitutively active) inhibited growth cone turning without reducing axon outgrowth velocity (Figure 8A-D).

claim: Shootin1 knockout mice have a penetrance of 69.2% for dysgenesis of corpus callosum, anterior commissure and hippocampal commissure.
source: Coronal and horizontal sections of Shootin1 knockout brains revealed dysgenesis of the corpus callosum, anterior commissure and hippocampal commissure with a penetrance of 69.2% (n = 26)
evidence: Histological analysis of brain sections from knockout mice (Figure 1C, D).

claim: 13.3% of Shootin1 knockout mice died during P0-P20.
source: Shootin1 knockout mice were born but 13.3% of them died during P0-P20 (n = 98).
evidence: Observation of survival rates in knockout mice colony.

claim: Shootin1a expression is low in embryonic day 13.5 mouse brains and increases remarkably between E13.5 and E16.5.
source: Consistent with a previous report (Toriyama et al., 2006), immunoblot analyses detected a low level of shootin1a in embryonic day (E) 13.5 mouse brains (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A). The expression increased remarkably between E13.5 and E16.5
evidence: Immunoblot analysis of shootin1a in mouse brain at various developmental stages (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).

claim: Shootin1a expression remains high through postnatal days 0-12 and then decreases to a low level in the adult.
source: The expression increased remarkably between E13.5 and E16.5, remained high through postnatal days (P) 0–12, and then decreased to a low level in the adult.
evidence: Immunoblot analysis showing developmental expression pattern (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).

claim: Shootin1a immunoreactivity was undetectable in the ventral commissure of the spinal cord at E12.
source: However, we could not detect shootin1a immunoreactivity in the ventral commissure of the spinal cord at E12 (arrow, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A)
evidence: Immunohistochemical analysis of E12.5 spinal cord sections (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).

claim: No noticeable defects of spinal cord commissure axons were observed in Shootin1 knockout mice.
source: Consistent with the undetectable level of shootin1a expression in the ventral commissure of the spinal cord (arrow, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), we could not observe noticeable defects of the spinal cord commissure axons in Shootin1 knockout mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B and C).
evidence: Immunohistochemical analysis and quantification of ventral spinal commissure thickness showed no significant difference between WT and KO (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B, C).

claim: The microfluidic device generated stable gradients of BSA with a 15% difference in concentration across 400 μm.
source: The difference in the BSA concentrations at the source side end and the other end of the area that expands 400 μm at the center of the linear gradient (red rectangle, Figure 2A), estimated by the fluorescence intensity, was 15% (Figure 2B).
evidence: Time-lapse fluorescence imaging of Alexa Fluor 488-BSA in the microfluidic device (Figure 2B, Video 1).

claim: The gradient steepness of netrin-1 covering growth cones is approximately 0.4%.
source: As the regular growth cone width of cultured hippocampal neurons is about 10 μm (Katsuno et al., 2015), we estimate that gradient steepness (the percentage change in concentration) (Rosoff et al., 2004) of netrin-1 that covers growth cones located in the red rectangle area (Figure 2A) is about 0.4%.
evidence: Calculation based on BSA gradient measurements and growth cone dimensions.

claim: The relative level of phosphorylated shootin1a was 71% higher on the netrin-1 source side than on the control side within growth cones.
source: The relative level of the phosphorylated shootin1a (phosopho-shootin1a immunoreactivity/CMAC staining) was 71% higher on the netrin-1 source side than on the control side (p=0.002, n = 12) (Figure 2D)
evidence: Quantification of phospho-shootin1a immunolabeling in growth cones exposed to netrin-1 gradients (Figure 2C, D).

claim: BSA gradients did not elicit polarized phosphorylation of shootin1 within growth cones.
source: On the other hand, similar gradients of the control molecule BSA in the medium did not elicit polarized phosphorylation of shootin1 within growth cones (Figure 2―figure supplement 2).
evidence: Immunolabeling and quantification of phospho-shootin1a in growth cones exposed to BSA gradients showed no significant difference (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).

claim: The apparent dissociation constant for shootin1a-DD binding to L1-CAM-ICD is 2.9-fold lower than that of shootin1a-WT.
source: the apparent dissociation constant for shootin1a-DD (Kd = 46.4 ± 4.4 nM) was 2.9-fold lower (p<0.02, n = 3 independent experiments) than that of shootin1a-WT (Kd = 133.5 ± 13.6 nM) (Figure 3C).
evidence: In vitro binding assay with increasing concentrations of shootin1a-DD and shootin1a-WT with L1-CAM-ICD (Figure 3B, C).

claim: Pak1 phosphorylation of shootin1a promotes its interaction with L1-CAM-ICD.
source: In vitro phosphorylation and binding assays also demonstrated that phosphorylation of shootin1a by Pak1 promotes its interaction with L1-CAM-ICD (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: In vitro kinase assay followed by binding assay showed increased interaction of Pak1-phosphorylated shootin1a with L1-CAM-ICD (Figure 3D, E).

claim: Expression of constitutively active Pak1 in HEK293T cells increased phosphorylation of myc-shootin1a at Ser101 and Ser249.
source: Ectopic expression of a constitutively active Pak1 in HEK293T cells increased phosphorylation of myc-shootin1a at Ser101 and Ser249 in these cells (Figure 4A and B)
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation and immunoblot analysis in HEK293T cells expressing constitutively active Pak1 (Figure 4A, B).

claim: Expression of dominant-negative Pak1 decreased shootin1a phosphorylation and inhibited shootin1a-L1-CAM interaction.
source: Conversely, expression of a dominant-negative Pak1 decreased shootin1a phosphorylation and inhibited the interaction (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation and immunoblot analysis in HEK293T cells expressing dominant-negative Pak1 (Figure 4A, B).

claim: Netrin-1 stimulation of neurons increased phosphorylation of shootin1a at Ser101 and Ser249.
source: Furthermore, stimulation of neurons by netrin-1 increased the phosphorylation of shootin1a at Ser101 and Ser249 (Figure 4C and D)
evidence: Immunoblot analysis of cortical neurons stimulated with netrin-1 (Figure 4C, D).

claim: Netrin-1 stimulation led to increased interaction between endogenous shootin1a and L1-CAM.
source: Furthermore, stimulation of neurons by netrin-1 increased the phosphorylation of shootin1a at Ser101 and Ser249 (Figure 4C and D); this led to a concomitant increase in the interaction between endogenous shootin1a and L1-CAM (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation analysis of cortical neurons stimulated with netrin-1 showed increased shootin1a-L1-CAM interaction (Figure 4C, D).

claim: Phosphorylated shootin1a is highly colocalized with L1-CAM in axonal growth cones.
source: In axonal growth cones, phosphorylated shootin1a was highly colocalized with L1-CAM (Figure 4E).
evidence: TIRF microscopy imaging of growth cones labeled with anti-pSer249-shootin1a and anti-L1-CAM antibodies (Figure 4E).

claim: Myc-shootin1a (1-125) is highly colocalized with L1-CAM in axonal growth cones.
source: Consistent with these data, when expressed in hippocampal neurons, myc-shootin1a (1-125) was highly colocalized with L1-CAM in axonal growth cones (Figure 5B).
evidence: Immunofluorescence imaging of neurons expressing myc-shootin1a (1-125) labeled with anti-myc and anti-L1-CAM antibodies (Figure 5B).

claim: Shootin1a (1-125) overexpressed in HEK293T cells inhibited the interaction between shootin1a and L1-CAM-ICD.
source: Indeed, shootin1a (1-125) overexpressed in HEK293T cells bound to L1-CAM-ICD, and inhibited the interaction between shootin1a and L1-CAM-ICD (Figure 5C).
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation assay in HEK293T cells overexpressing shootin1a (1-125) (Figure 5C).

claim: Overexpression of myc-shootin1a (1-125) increased the velocity of F-actin flow in hippocampal neurons.
source: Overexpression of myc-shootin1a (1-125) in hippocampal neurons increased the velocity of F-actin flow (Figure 6A and B)
evidence: Fluorescent speckle imaging of mRFP-actin in growth cones overexpressing myc-shootin1a (1-125) (Figure 6A, B, Video 2).

claim: Netrin-1 stimulation significantly decreased the velocity of F-actin flow in control growth cones.
source: Netrin-1 stimulation significantly decreased the velocity of F-actin flow in control growth cones, reflecting promotion of the F-actin–adhesion coupling.
evidence: Fluorescent speckle imaging showing reduced F-actin flow velocity after netrin-1 stimulation in control neurons (Figure 6A, B).

claim: Netrin-1 accelerated F-actin flow in the presence of overexpressed myc-shootin1a (1-125).
source: On the other hand, netrin-1 accelerated the flow in the presence of overexpressed myc-shootin1a (1-125) (Figure 6A and B)
evidence: Fluorescent speckle imaging showing increased F-actin flow velocity after netrin-1 stimulation in neurons overexpressing shootin1a (1-125) (Figure 6A, B).

claim: Netrin-1 stimulation significantly increased traction forces under growth cones.
source: As reported (Toriyama et al., 2013), the reporter beads under the growth cones moved dynamically, reflecting the traction force on the substrate (Figure 6C, Video 3); and the force was increased significantly by netrin-1 stimulation (Figure 6C and D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Traction force microscopy showing increased bead displacement after netrin-1 stimulation (Figure 6C, D, Video 3).

claim: Overexpression of myc-shootin1a (1-125) decreased axon length and abolished netrin-1–induced axon outgrowth.
source: Overexpression of myc-shootin1a (1-125) also decreased axon length and abolished the netrin-1–induced axon outgrowth (Figure 6―figure supplement 1B and Figure 6E)
evidence: Measurement of axon length in neurons overexpressing shootin1a (1-125) with and without netrin-1 stimulation (Figure 6E, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).

claim: The mean axon outgrowth velocity in control hippocampal neurons under netrin-1 gradients was 24.4 μm/h.
source: The mean axon outgrowth velocity was 24.4 ± 0.7 μm/h (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: Time-lapse imaging and tracking of axonal growth cones under netrin-1 gradients (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A, B, Video 4).

claim: The net change in the angle of growth cones toward the netrin-1 source was 26.4° in control conditions.
source: the net change in the angle of the growth cone toward the netrin-1 source was 26.4 ± 0.1° (n = 9) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Analysis of growth cone turning angles from time-lapse imaging (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A, C).

claim: Inclusion of 2 μg/ml heparin in the culture medium released netrin-1 from the L1-CAM–coated substrate.
source: As in the case of polylysine–coated substrate (Moore et al., 2012), inclusion of 2 μg/ml heparin in the culture medium released netrin-1 from the L1-CAM–coated substrate (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: Immunofluorescence analysis of netrin-1 attachment to substrates with and without heparin (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B).

claim: Netrin-1 gradient induced axon turning even in the presence of heparin.
source: In contrast to the data obtained with spinal cord neurons (Moore et al., 2012), the netrin-1 gradient induced axon turning even in the presence of heparin, indicating that a gradient of soluble netrin-1 contributes to axon turning of hippocampal neurons (Figure 7―figure supplement 1D, Video 5).
evidence: Time-lapse imaging of hippocampal neurons under netrin-1 gradients with heparin (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D, Video 5).

claim: The degree of netrin-1–induced axon outgrowth and turning was reduced in the presence of heparin.
source: However, the degree of netrin-1–induced axon outgrowth and turning was reduced in the presence of heparin (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: Quantification of axon outgrowth velocity and turning angle with and without heparin (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B, C).

claim: Gradients of both soluble and substrate-bound netrin-1 contribute to axon turning of hippocampal neurons.
source: Thus, we conclude that gradients of both soluble and substrate-bound netrin-1 contribute to axon turning of hippocampal neurons in our assay system.
evidence: Experiments with and without heparin showing both forms contribute to axon turning (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).

claim: Repression of shootin1a by RNAi reduced axon outgrowth velocity from 26.1 to 5.6 μm/h.
source: Repression of shootin1a by RNAi not only reduced the axon outgrowth velocity (5.6 ± 0.9 μm/h, p<0.01) (Figure 7B and C, Video 7)
evidence: Time-lapse imaging and quantification of axon outgrowth in neurons expressing shootin1a miRNA (Figure 7B, C, Video 7).

claim: Repression of shootin1a by RNAi inhibited growth cone turning toward the netrin-1 source from 32.7° to 2.1°.
source: Repression of shootin1a by RNAi not only reduced the axon outgrowth velocity (5.6 ± 0.9 μm/h, p<0.01) (Figure 7B and C, Video 7) but also inhibited the growth cone turning toward the netrin-1 source (2.1 ± 1.2°, p<0.01, n = 13) (Figure 7B and D).
evidence: Analysis of turning angles in neurons expressing shootin1a miRNA under netrin-1 gradients (Figure 7B, D).

claim: Shootin1 knockout neurons showed similar defects in axon outgrowth and turning as RNAi knockdown.
source: Similar results were obtained using hippocampal neurons prepared from Shootin1 knockout mice (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Time-lapse imaging and quantification of axon outgrowth and turning in Shootin1 knockout neurons (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).

claim: Inhibition of shootin1a–L1-CAM interaction by overexpressing EGFP-shootin1a (1-125) reduced axon outgrowth velocity from 32.4 to 13.8 μm/h.
source: On the other hand, inhibition of the shootin1a–L1-CAM interaction by overexpressing EGFP-shootin1a (1-125) not only reduced the axon outgrowth velocity (13.8 ± 3.4 μm/h, p<0.05)
evidence: Time-lapse imaging and quantification of axon outgrowth in neurons overexpressing EGFP-shootin1a (1-125) (Figure 7F, Figure 7—figure supplement 3A).

claim: Inhibition of shootin1a–L1-CAM interaction by overexpressing EGFP-shootin1a (1-125) inhibited growth cone turning toward the netrin-1 source from 28.8° to 0.6°.
source: On the other hand, inhibition of the shootin1a–L1-CAM interaction by overexpressing EGFP-shootin1a (1-125) not only reduced the axon outgrowth velocity (13.8 ± 3.4 μm/h, p<0.05) but also inhibited the growth cone turning toward the netrin-1 source (0.6 ± 1.1°, p<0.01, n = 16) (Figure 7F, Figure 7—figure supplement 3 and Video 9).
evidence: Analysis of turning angles in neurons overexpressing EGFP-shootin1a (1-125) (Figure 7F, Figure 7—figure supplement 3B).

claim: Growth cones of cultured hippocampal neurons on laminin turned in response to netrin-1 gradients.
source: Growth cones of cultured hippocampal neurons on laminin turned in response to netrin-1 gradients (Figure 7—figure supplement 4A–C), as they did on L1-CAM (Figure 7―figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Time-lapse imaging of neurons on laminin substrate under netrin-1 gradients (Figure 7—figure supplement 4A-C).

claim: The F-actin retrograde flow rate in control growth cones on laminin was 2.3 μm/min.
source: Consistent with previously reported data (Abe et al., 2018), the F-actin retrograde flow rate in control growth cones on laminin was 2.3 ± 0.3 μm/min (Figure 7—figure supplement 4D).
evidence: Fluorescent speckle imaging of mRFP-actin in growth cones on laminin (Figure 7—figure supplement 4D).

claim: Overexpression of shootin1a (1-125) increased F-actin retrograde flow rate in growth cones on laminin.
source: As in the case of growth cones on L1-CAM (Figure 6A and B), overexpression of shootin1a (1-125) increased significantly the retrograde flow rate under these conditions (Figure 7—figure supplement 4D)
evidence: Fluorescent speckle imaging showing increased F-actin flow in growth cones on laminin overexpressing shootin1a (1-125) (Figure 7—figure supplement 4D).

claim: Uncoupling of F-actin-adhesion coupling by shootin1a (1-125) inhibited netrin-1–induced axon outgrowth and turning on laminin.
source: Furthermore, uncoupling of F-actin-adhesion coupling by shootin1a (1-125) inhibited netrin-1–induced axon outgrowth and turning on laminin (Figure 7—figure supplement 4A–C and E).
evidence: Time-lapse imaging and quantification of axon outgrowth and turning in neurons on laminin overexpressing shootin1a (1-125) (Figure 7—figure supplement 4A-C, E).

claim: Expression of RNAi-refractory shootin1a-WT in neurons expressing shootin1a miRNA rescued the reduction of axon outgrowth and growth cone turning.
source: Expression of RNAi-refractory shootin1a-WT in neurons expressing shootin1a miRNA rescued the reduction of axon outgrowth as well as growth cone turning (Figure 8A, C and D, Video 10)
evidence: Time-lapse imaging and quantification showing rescue of axon outgrowth and turning by RNAi-refractory shootin1a-WT (Figure 8A, C, D, Video 10).

claim: Displacement of wild-type shootin1a with shootin1a-DD inhibited growth cone turning toward the netrin-1 source without reducing axon outgrowth velocity.
source: As shown by Figure 8B–D and Video 11, disturbance of polarized shootin1a phosphorylation within growth cones by this displacement inhibited growth cone turning toward the netrin-1 source without reducing axon outgrowth velocity.
evidence: Time-lapse imaging and quantification showing that shootin1a-DD expression inhibited turning but not outgrowth (Figure 8B-D, Video 11).

claim: Netrin-1 is one of the best-characterized axon guidance molecules.
source: Netrin-1 is one of the best-characterized axon guidance molecules (Ishii et al., 1992; Serafini et al., 1994; Lai Wing Sun et al., 2011).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to foundational netrin-1 research.

claim: Extracellular gradients of netrin-1 elicit growth cone attraction in vitro.
source: Extracellular gradients of netrin-1 elicit growth cone attraction in vitro (Kennedy et al., 1994; Serafini et al., 1994; Hong et al., 1999; Bhattacharjee et al., 2010; Fothergill et al., 2014).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to studies demonstrating netrin-1-induced attraction.

claim: Mice lacking netrin-1 or DCC show impaired projection and guidance of axons in the ventral spinal commissure and forebrain commissures.
source: Mice lacking netrin-1 or its receptor deleted in colorectal cancer (DCC) show impaired projection and guidance of axons in the ventral spinal commissure and forebrain commissures (Serafini et al., 1996; Fazeli et al., 1997; Bin et al., 2015; Yung et al., 2015).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to knockout mouse studies.

claim: Stimulation of DCC by netrin-1 activates Cdc42 and Rac1 and their downstream kinase Pak1.
source: For example, stimulation of DCC by netrin-1 activates Cdc42 and Rac1 and their downstream kinase Pak1, thereby inducing growth cone expansion and axon extension (Li et al., 2002; Shekarabi and Kennedy, 2002; Shekarabi et al., 2005; Briançon-Marjollet et al., 2008; Demarco et al., 2012).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to signaling pathway studies.

claim: Shootin1a interacts with F-actin retrograde flow via cortactin.
source: Shootin1a interacts with F-actin retrograde flow via cortactin (Weed and Parsons, 2001) and couples the F-actin flow with extracellular adhesive substrates (Shimada et al., 2008; Kubo et al., 2015) through the cell adhesion molecule L1-CAM (Rathjen and Schachner, 1984; Kamiguchi et al., 1998).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to previous studies on shootin1a function.

claim: Pak1 phosphorylates shootin1a upon activation by netrin-1.
source: We previously reported that Pak1 (Manser et al., 1994), upon activation by netrin-1, phosphorylates shootin1a (Toriyama et al., 2013)
evidence: Statement refers to previous work by the authors.

claim: Shootin1a phosphorylation enhances shootin1a interaction with F-actin flow, thereby producing traction force on the substrate.
source: We previously reported that Pak1 (Manser et al., 1994), upon activation by netrin-1, phosphorylates shootin1a (Toriyama et al., 2013); this in turn enhances shootin1a interaction with F-actin flow, thereby producing traction force on the substrate (Toriyama et al., 2013; Kubo et al., 2015).
evidence: Statement refers to previous work by the authors.

claim: Growth cones can navigate in response to extremely shallow gradients of diffusible and substrate-bound chemical cues.
source: Furthermore, analyses with microfluidic devices have shown that growth cones can navigate in response to extremely shallow gradients of diffusible and substrate-bound chemical cues in the microenvironment (Baier and Bonhoeffer, 1992; Rosoff et al., 2004; Xiao et al., 2014).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to microfluidic studies.

claim: At the leading edge of growth cones, F-actins polymerize and disassemble proximally, thereby undergoing retrograde flow.
source: At the leading edge of growth cones, actin filaments (F-actins) polymerize and disassemble proximally, thereby undergoing retrograde flow (Forscher and Smith, 1988; Katoh et al., 1999).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to foundational studies on F-actin dynamics.

claim: Coupling between F-actins and substrate reduces the speed of F-actin flow in growth cones.
source: Coupling between F-actins and substrate reduces the speed of F-actin flow in growth cones (Suter et al., 1998; Toriyama et al., 2013).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to studies on F-actin-substrate coupling.

claim: L1-CAM on growth cones interacts directly with laminin presented on the substrate.
source: Laminins are widely used substrates for axon guidance assays (Turney and Bridgman, 2005; Nichol et al., 2016); L1-CAM on growth cones interacts directly with laminin presented on the substrate (Hall et al., 1997; Abe et al., 2018).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to studies on L1-CAM-laminin interaction.

claim: Netrin-1 attaches to polylysine–coated substrates.
source: A previous study reported that netrin-1 attaches to polylysine–coated substrates, thereby mediating chemotropic axon guidance (Moore et al., 2012).
evidence: Statement refers to a previous study on netrin-1 substrate attachment.

claim: The molecular weight of BSA (66.0 kDa) is similar to that of mouse netrin-1 (68.2 kDa).
source: As the molecular weight of BSA (66.0 kDa) is similar to that of mouse netrin-1 (68.2 kDa), we expect that the gradient of BSA mimics that of netrin-1 in the device.
evidence: Statement based on known molecular weights of proteins.

claim: The regular growth cone width of cultured hippocampal neurons is about 10 μm.
source: As the regular growth cone width of cultured hippocampal neurons is about 10 μm (Katsuno et al., 2015)
evidence: Statement supported by citation to previous measurement.

claim: Shootin1a residues 261-377 are responsible for interaction with cortactin.
source: On the other hand, we previously reported that another region, shootin1a (261-377), is responsible for its interaction with cortactin, which links shootin1a to F-actin flow (Figure 5A) (Kubo et al., 2015).
evidence: Statement refers to previous work by the authors.

claim: Shootin1a-DD mediates clutch coupling and force generation in the absence of PAK1 activity.
source: As shootin1a-DD, the constitutively active shootin1a, mediates clutch coupling and force generation in the absence of PAK1 activity (Toriyama et al., 2013)
evidence: Statement refers to previous work by the authors.

claim: Netrin-1 mRNA is distributed along the paths of forebrain commissural axons.
source: However, although netrin-1 mRNA is distributed along the paths of forebrain commissural axons (Serafini et al., 1996), netrin-1 gradients have not yet been reported in these brain regions.
evidence: Statement supported by citation to netrin-1 expression study.

claim: Netrin-1 locally presented by neural progenitors is required for guidance of spinal commissural axons.
source: On the other hand, recent studies reported that netrin-1 locally presented by neural progenitors is required for guidance of the spinal commissural axons (Dominici et al., 2017; Varadarajan et al., 2017)
evidence: Statement supported by citations to recent studies on netrin-1 presentation.

claim: Spinal commissural axons respond to substrate-bound netrin-1 and steep gradients of netrin-1 in vitro.
source: On the other hand, recent studies reported that netrin-1 locally presented by neural progenitors is required for guidance of the spinal commissural axons (Dominici et al., 2017; Varadarajan et al., 2017) and that these axons respond to substrate-bound netrin-1 (Moore et al., 2012) and steep gradients of netrin-1 (Sloan et al., 2015) in vitro.
evidence: Statement supported by citations to in vitro studies.

claim: Immobilized netrin-1 plays a key role in mechanical activation of FAK for axonal haptotaxis.
source: Concerning the axon guidance mechanism of these neurons, Moore et al. (2012) reported that immobilization of netrin-1 is required; the immobilized netrin-1 is proposed to play a key role in mechanical activation of FAK, thereby leading to activation of signaling pathways including Crk-associated substrate (CAS) for axonal haptotaxis.
evidence: Statement refers to proposed mechanism from cited study.

claim: Shootin1 knockout mice exhibit multiple defects in the brain.
source: In addition, as Shootin1 knockout mice exhibit multiple defects in the brain, we cannot conclude that the dysgenesis of the forebrain commissures is only due to the axon outgrowth and guidance deficits observed in in vitro assays.
evidence: Observation from histological analysis of knockout mice brains.

claim: Shootin1 knockout mice showed agenesis of the septum.
source: We also observed multiple defects in the brain of Shootin1 knockout mice, including agenesis of the septum (Figure 1C)
evidence: Histological observation in knockout mice brain sections.

claim: The thickness of corpus callosum, hippocampal commissure, and anterior commissure were significantly reduced in Shootin1 knockout mice.
source: Coronal and horizontal sections of Shootin1 knockout brains revealed dysgenesis of the corpus callosum, anterior commissure and hippocampal commissure with a penetrance of 69.2% (n = 26) (Figure 1C and D and Figure 1―figure supplement 1C); their thicknesses were significantly reduced by Shootin1 knockout (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of commissure thickness in Nissl-stained sections (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).

claim: At least 61% of the applied netrin-1 is not attached to the L1-CAM-coated substrate under the experimental conditions.
source: However, the amount of attached netrin-1 was 39% of that on polylysine after 420 min incubation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B), suggesting that at least 61% of the applied netrin-1 is not attached to the substrate under our conditions.
evidence: Quantification of netrin-1 attachment to different substrates (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B).

claim: The gradient steepness of netrin-1 attached to substrate is about 0.6% at 10 min and 0.8% at 430 min.
source: We also confirmed that our device produces a netrin-1 gradient attached to the substrate in a manner dependent on the incubation time and that the difference in concentration across the growth cone is about 0.6% at 10 min and 0.8% at 430 min (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: Immunofluorescence analysis of netrin-1 attached to substrate over time (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).

claim: The disturbance of axon turning caused by depletion of shootin1a is not attributed only to inhibited axon outgrowth.
source: These results demonstrate that the disturbance of axon turning caused by depletion of shootin1a (Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 2D) or by dominant negative shootin1a (Figure 7—figure supplement 3B) is not attributed only to the inhibited axon outgrowth
evidence: Comparison of effects of shootin1a-WT rescue versus shootin1a-DD on axon outgrowth and turning (Figure 8A-D).

claim: Shootin1a constitutes a gradient-reading and mechano-effector machinery involved in netrin-1–induced axon guidance.
source: These results suggest that shootin1a constitutes a gradient-reading and mechano-effector machinery involved in netrin-1–induced axon guidance.
evidence: Integration of findings showing polarized phosphorylation, enhanced L1-CAM interaction, increased traction force, and requirement for axon turning.

claim: The polarized phosphorylation of shootin1a within growth cones is required for the directional axon guidance induced by netrin-1 gradients.
source: These results demonstrate that the disturbance of axon turning caused by depletion of shootin1a (Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 2D) or by dominant negative shootin1a (Figure 7—figure supplement 3B) is not attributed only to the inhibited axon outgrowth, and suggest that the polarized phosphorylation of shootin1a within growth cones is required for the directional axon guidance induced by netrin-1 gradients (Figure 8E).
evidence: Experiments showing shootin1a-DD expression inhibits turning but not outgrowth (Figure 8B-D).

claim: Netrin-1–induced shootin1a phosphorylation promotes direct interaction between shootin1a and L1-CAM, thereby generating traction force for growth cone motility.
source: Netrin-1–elicited shootin1a phosphorylation promoted direct interaction between shootin1a and L1-CAM, thereby generating traction force for growth cone motility.
evidence: Integration of binding assays, traction force measurements, and functional studies.

claim: Shootin1a, through its spatially regulated phosphorylation within growth cones, mediates the gradient reading and mechanoresponse for netrin-1–induced axon guidance.
source: Our data demonstrate that shootin1a, through its spatially regulated phosphorylation within growth cones, mediates the gradient reading and mechanoresponse for netrin-1–induced axon guidance.
evidence: Integration of all experimental findings on polarized phosphorylation, mechanical coupling, and directional guidance.
